title: 1833: Chicago is born
hook: In August 1833, Chicago became a town of about 350 people. Just 4 years later, on March 4, 1837, it became a city, and its first census that July counted 4,170 residents.
facts: Then it really took off. By 1890, Chicago had passed 1 million people and become the 2nd-largest city in the US, one of the fastest-growing cities in the world.
From a muddy settlement at the river to a giant in about 60 years. Follow along for more Chicago Story

title: Chicago is named after… an onion? Pretty much
hook: "Chicago" comes from the Miami-Illinois word šikaakwa (shikaakwa). It means the wild leek, or ramp (Allium tricoccum), a pungent wild cousin of the onion and garlic that grew along the river. The same word was also used for the striped skunk. You can guess why.
facts: In September 1687 the French explorer Henri Joutel wrote that the place "called Chicagou" got its name "because of the quantity of garlic which grows in the forests in this region." French maps spelled it many ways: Checagou, Chicagou, Chekagou… and eventually Chicago.
So yes, the big city is named after a very smelly wild onion.

title: October 8, 1871. Chicago burns
hook: The fire broke out on a Sunday night on the city's West Side and burned until early Tuesday, October 10, about two days. When it was over, about 3.3 square miles (2,100+ acres) of the city were gone, including some 17,500 buildings and the heart of downtown.
facts: About 300 people died, and roughly 100,000 people, about one in three Chicagoans, lost their homes.

And the cow? Legend says Mrs. O'Leary's cow kicked over a lantern. But the cause was never determined, reporter Michael Ahern admitted in 1893 that the cow story was made up, and in 1997 the Chicago City Council officially cleared Catherine O'Leary and her cow.

title: From ashes to the sky
hook: After the 1871 fire, Chicago didn't just rebuild. It built up. Lumber for new buildings arrived the day the last flames died, and in 1872 the city drew "fire limits" downtown where new buildings had to be brick or stone. Architects poured in, and what became the Chicago School of architecture was born.
facts: In 1885, at LaSalle & Adams, William Le Baron Jenney's Home Insurance Building opened: 10 stories, about 138 feet, on a fireproofed iron-and-steel frame that carried much of the building's weight. Two more floors were added in 1891. It's often called the world's first skyscraper, though historians still debate that title. It was torn down in 1931.
By 1893, just 22 years after the fire, Chicago hosted the World's Columbian Exposition, with 27.5 million admissions.

title: The river that flows backwards
hook: Chicago's sewers once drained into the Chicago River, and the river emptied into Lake Michigan, the city's drinking water. After a huge storm in 1885 washed river filth far into the lake, the fear of disease was enough: in 1889 the state created the Sanitary District.
facts: (About that "90,000 people died in 1885" story you may have heard: it's a myth. No such epidemic happened.)

The fix was bold. Engineers dug the 28-mile Sanitary and Ship Canal, at the time the largest earth-moving project in North America. In January 1900 it opened, and the river reversed, sending the sewage inland toward the Illinois and Mississippi rivers, away from the lake.
Downstream wasn't thrilled: Missouri sued, and in 1906 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled for Illinois. In 1999 civil engineers named the system a "Monument of the Millennium."
And since 1962, the plumbers union has dyed the river green every year for St. Patrick's Day.

title: Chicago got the blues, and the jazz
hook: In 1922 a young cornet player from New Orleans stepped off the train in Chicago to join King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band: Louis Armstrong. From 1925 to 1928 he made his first records as a bandleader here for OKeh, with the Hot Five and Hot Seven: about sixty recordings that transformed jazz.
facts: Two decades later, in 1943, Muddy Waters came up from Mississippi. In 1948 his single "I Can't Be Satisfied" on Aristocrat Records became a hit. In 1950 brothers Leonard and Phil Chess renamed the label Chess Records, and Muddy recorded for them until 1975, landing 16 top-20 R&B hits, including Willie Dixon's "I'm Your Hoochie Coochie Man." Many call him the Father of Chicago Blues.
From the South Side to the world: you can hear Chicago blues in the Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin and beyond.

title: Chicago today: one of a kind
hook: From a muddy portage to a world city. Today Chicago is the third-largest city in the US, with about 2.7 million people.
facts: Willis Tower: 1,451 ft and 110 stories, the world's tallest building when it opened in 1973.
The 'L': the first elevated line opened in 1892, and part of it still runs as today's Green Line.
Deep dish: first served in 1943 at the spot now called Pizzeria Uno. Who invented it? Still debated.
26 miles of Lake Michigan shoreline, mostly public parks and free beaches.
extra: That's the end of our story, for now. Thanks for following 312 History from the first settler to the city of today. Which chapter was your favorite?

title: The city that lifted itself
hook: In the 1850s–60s Chicago raised its streets, then jacked whole buildings up to meet them.
facts: Flat, low land on clay soil left the streets muddy and poorly drained.
Ellis Chesbrough's 1856 sewer plan raised streets about 4–5 ft, up to 8 ft in places.
In 1861 the six-story Tremont House was raised about 6 ft while guests stayed inside.
In 1860 a row of Lake Street buildings rose 4 ft 8 in in five days, using 600 men and 6,000 jackscrews. Shops stayed open.
extra:
Myth or fact? "George Pullman lifted Chicago by himself."
Partly. Pullman made his name raising buildings, including the Tremont House, but many contractors and thousands of workers did the job.

title: The tower that survived
hook: In 1871 the Great Fire burned all around it. The Water Tower is still standing.
facts: Built in 1869 by W. W. Boyington from Joliet limestone, it hid a 138-ft standpipe that steadied the water pressure.
The fire of October 1871 swept through the North Side, but the stone tower held.
The pumping station across the street lost its roof and pumps, and city water was nearly cut off for about 8 days.
It survived demolition plans in 1906 and 1918, so Michigan Avenue bends around it. It became a city landmark in 1971.
extra:
Myth or fact? "It was the only building to survive the fire."
Myth. A few others survived in the burned area, including the pumping station's walls, St. Michael's Church and a police officer's cottage.

title: The Chicago window
hook: One big pane, two small ones that open: how Chicago gave skyscrapers their big windows.
facts: A Chicago window is a wide fixed pane between two narrow sashes that open for air, a must before air conditioning.
Steel frames carried the weight, so walls no longer had to be thick and windows could grow.
The Reliance Building, begun by Burnham & Root in 1890 and finished by Charles Atwood in 1895, is almost all glass and terra cotta. Its top ten floors went up in about 15 days.
Louis Sullivan's Schlesinger & Mayer store (1899–1904) paired Chicago windows with cast-iron ornament.
extra:
Myth or fact? "The Chicago window was invented for the Reliance."
Myth. The Reliance made it famous, but similar windows appeared in the 1880s, often credited to Jenney's Home Insurance Building.

title: The Prairie School
hook: Low roofs, long lines: a new American house was born around Chicago.
facts: Frank Lloyd Wright built his Oak Park home in 1889 and added a studio in 1898. Over 150 projects were designed there.
Prairie houses stress long, low lines, deep overhanging roofs and bands of windows that echo the flat Midwest.
The Robie House (designed 1908, finished 1910) is the high point of the style.
In 2019 Robie House and Oak Park's Unity Temple joined UNESCO's World Heritage List with six other Wright works.
extra:
Myth or fact? "Wright created the Prairie School alone."
Partly. Wright led it, but his studio team, including Marion Mahony (the first practicing woman architect in Illinois) and Walter Burley Griffin, shaped it too.

title: Tunnels under the Loop
hook: A hidden railway once ran about 40 ft under downtown Chicago.
facts: It began with an 1899 franchise for telephone cables. Tunnel digging started in 1900.
Freight service began in 1906, and the network reached about 60 miles by 1909.
Small electric trains on two-foot track carried rail freight, store packages, coal for boilers and ash for lakefront fill.
Abandoned in 1959, a tunnel under the river was punctured on April 13, 1992, flooding about two dozen Loop buildings.
extra:
Myth or fact? "They were planned as freight tunnels from day one."
Unclear. The 1899 franchise was for telephone cables. Whether trains were the plan all along is still debated.

title: The White City, 1893
hook: For six months Chicago built a dream city by the lake. Then most of it vanished.
facts: The World's Columbian Exposition filled about 600 acres of Jackson Park. Chicago beat New York, Washington and St. Louis to host it.
Under director of works Daniel Burnham, grand Beaux-Arts halls were covered in plaster and painted white: the "White City."
Open May 1 – Oct 30, 1893: 27,529,400 admissions in 179 days.
The Palace of Fine Arts became the Field Museum's first home and was later rebuilt as today's Museum of Science and Industry.
extra:
Myth or fact? "H. H. Holmes murdered hundreds of fair visitors."
Myth. Historians link him to about nine murders and find no evidence he killed fair-goers. The "murder castle" tales came from 1890s tabloids.

title: The first Ferris Wheel, 1893
hook: Chicago needed something to beat Paris's Eiffel Tower. An engineer from Pittsburgh had an idea.
facts: George W. G. Ferris's wheel took its first riders on June 21, 1893, at the World's Columbian Exposition: 250 ft across and about 264 ft tall.
36 cars, each with 40 seats and room for up to 60 people.
50 cents bought two turns. The wheel paid for itself by September 1, 1893.
It was rebuilt on the North Side in 1895, shipped to St. Louis for the 1904 fair, and dynamited in 1906.
extra:
Myth or fact? "The wheel made George Ferris a rich man."
Myth. Lawsuits over profits and a hard economy ruined him. He died in 1896, aged 37, nearly broke.

title: The Eastland, 1915
hook: Chicago's deadliest day happened in the river, steps from the shore.
facts: On the morning of July 24, 1915, Western Electric workers and their families boarded the SS Eastland for a company picnic trip to Michigan City, Indiana.
The ship had reached its capacity of about 2,500 passengers.
At 7:28 a.m., still tied up in the Chicago River between Clark and LaSalle, it rolled onto its side in about 20 ft of water.
844 people died, including 22 entire families. Many were young immigrant workers.
extra:
Myth or fact? "The Eastland sank far out in Lake Michigan."
Myth. It never left the dock. It overturned in the river, in the heart of the city, still tied to the wharf.

Had you heard of the Eastland before? Share it so they are remembered.

title: A Century of Progress, 1933
hook: In the middle of the Great Depression, Chicago threw a world's fair.
facts: It opened May 27, 1933, on Northerly Island and the lakefront for Chicago's 100th birthday: about 424 acres, much of it landfill.
The Sky Ride: two 628-ft towers, 1,850 ft apart, with "rocket cars" running between them.
George Fred Keck's glass House of Tomorrow, complete with an airplane hangar, now stands in the Indiana Dunes.
The fair was so popular it ran a second season in 1934: about 39 million visits in all.
extra:

title: The Big Snow, 1967
hook: Two days after a 65°F day, Chicago was buried under 23 inches of snow.
facts: Jan 24, 1967: a record 65°F, with thunderstorms that night. Then a cold front arrived.
Snow began at 5:02 a.m. on Thursday, Jan 26, and fell for about 29 hours. Winds off the lake gusted over 50 mph, with drifts of 4 to 6 feet.
23 inches in all: still Chicago's biggest snowstorm on record.
Thousands of cars and buses were stranded, O'Hare closed, and helicopters flew food and medicine in. Sadly, about 60 people in the Chicago area died because of the storm.
extra:
Myth or fact? "A snowstorm once cost a Chicago mayor his job."
Fact. After a slow cleanup from the 1979 blizzard, Mayor Michael Bilandic lost the Democratic primary to Jane Byrne, and many people blamed the snow.

title: Jane Addams & Hull House
hook: A house on the Near West Side changed how America helps its neighbors.
facts: In September 1889, Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr moved into an old mansion and opened Hull House.
Most neighbors were new immigrants. They came for kindergarten, classes, clubs, music and art.
Hull House grew into a complex of 13 buildings, with a gym, a theater and a coffee house.
In 1931 Jane Addams became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
extra:
Myth or fact? "Jane Addams built Hull House."
Myth. The house was built in 1856 for Charles Hull. Addams and Starr moved in and opened it to the whole neighborhood. Today it is the Jane Addams Hull-House Museum.

title: Ida B. Wells
hook: She used a pen to fight injustice, and Chicago became her home base.
facts: Born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi, in 1862, she became a teacher, then a journalist and newspaper owner in Memphis.
In 1892, after three of her friends were murdered by a mob, she investigated lynching and published the facts in "Southern Horrors."
She moved to Chicago in 1893 and married lawyer Ferdinand Barnett in 1895.
She helped found the NAACP in 1909 and started the Alpha Suffrage Club in 1913 to win the vote for Black women. In 2020 she received a special Pulitzer Prize citation.
extra:
Myth or fact? "She refused to give up her train seat 71 years before Rosa Parks."
Fact. In 1884 she was dragged off a train for refusing to leave the ladies' car. She sued the railroad and won, but a higher court overturned the decision.

title: Al Capone: Myth vs Fact
hook: America's most famous gangster went to prison for taxes — not murder.
facts: Prohibition (1920–1933) banned selling alcohol. Illegal liquor made gangs rich, and the city violent.
Capone, born in Brooklyn in 1899, came to run a violent Chicago gang.
Federal agents followed the money. In October 1931 he was convicted of tax evasion and sentenced to 11 years.
He was sent to Alcatraz in 1934, released in 1939, and died in 1947.
extra:
Myth or fact? "Capone went to prison for the St. Valentine's Day Massacre."
Myth. No one was ever convicted for the 1929 killings. Capone went to prison for not paying his taxes.

title: The Burnham Plan, 1909
hook: In 1909, one bold plan re-drew Chicago — and much of it came true.
facts: In July 1909, Daniel Burnham and Edward Bennett published the Plan of Chicago for the Commercial Club.
Artist Jules Guérin painted dreamy watercolor views of the future city.
Many ideas came true: a long chain of lakefront parks, Wacker Drive, the Michigan Avenue bridge and Northerly Island.
Not all of it came true: the giant domed civic center was never built.
"Make no little plans" — Burnham said these famous words in London in 1910. They are not in the 1909 Plan.

title: Bessie Coleman
hook: No flight school in America would teach her. So she learned in France.
facts: Born in Texas in 1892, she moved to Chicago and worked as a manicurist.
Flight schools in the US turned her away because she was Black and a woman.
Chicago Defender publisher Robert S. Abbott backed her. She trained at Le Crotoy in France.
On June 15, 1921, she got an international pilot's license — the first African American woman, and the first Native American, to hold one.
Known as "Queen Bess," she thrilled crowds at air shows. She died in a plane crash in 1926, at 34.

title: Bronzeville & the Great Migration
hook: Half a million Black Southerners came to Chicago, and built a city within a city.
facts: From 1916 to 1970, just over 500,000 African Americans moved to Chicago from the South.
The Chicago Defender, founded by Robert S. Abbott in 1905, urged readers in the South to come north.
Chicago's Black population grew from about 44,000 in 1910 to about 234,000 in 1930.
Shut out by segregation, residents built their own banks, churches, newspapers and theaters: the "Black Metropolis."
The community gave Bronzeville its own name. James J. Gentry of the Chicago Bee coined it around 1930.

title: Pullman: The Company Town
hook: A railroad-car king built a "perfect" town. It ended in a national strike.
facts: From 1880 to 1884, George Pullman built a model town for the workers at his railroad-car factory.
The company owned every house and shop, and the rents had to earn it a profit.
In the 1893 depression, Pullman cut wages but not rents. On May 11, 1894, workers went on strike.
Rail workers across the country boycotted Pullman cars: about 250,000 workers in 27 states. Federal troops ended the strike by mid-July.
The strike pushed Congress to make Labor Day a national holiday in June 1894 — 31 states already had one. In 2015, Pullman became a National Monument.

title: The Stockyards & 'The Jungle'
hook: For more than 100 years, one giant yard fed America — and changed its food laws.
facts: The Union Stock Yard opened on Christmas Day 1865.
It covered 475 acres and handled more than one billion animals before it closed in 1971.
Around 1921, about 40,000 people worked there, many of them immigrants.

In 1906 Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle shocked readers. That same year, Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act. Sinclair wanted to help workers: "I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach."
Carl Sandburg called Chicago "Hog Butcher for the World" in his poem "Chicago" (1914).

title: Pilsen: From Bohemia to Mexico
hook: One Chicago neighborhood, two homelands: first Bohemia, then Mexico.
facts: After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, Bohemian (Czech) immigrants settled along 18th Street. A restaurant called "At the City of Plzen" honored Plzen in Bohemia, and people began calling the area Pilsen.
St Procopius parish was organized in 1875 for Czech Catholics. Its big Romanesque church was dedicated in 1883 and still stands as a link to Bohemian Pilsen.

In the 1950s and 1960s, many Mexican families moved to Pilsen. Some were pushed out of the Near West Side by expressways and the new University of Illinois campus. By 1970, Mexican-born residents were nearly half of Pilsen.
From the 1960s and 1970s, murals, signs and bright colors brought Mexican culture to the old Bohemian buildings. In 2006 the Pilsen Historic District joined the National Register of Historic Places.
In 1982, teacher Carlos Tortolero and other educators founded a Mexican art museum. It opened in Pilsen in 1987 and is now the National Museum of Mexican Art.

title: Polish Chicago
hook: One of the great Polish cities outside Poland grew up around a Chicago church.
facts: Polish Downtown grew around the Polish Triangle, where Division, Ashland and Milwaukee meet. In 1867, St Stanislaus Kostka became Chicago's first Polish parish.
The biggest Polish wave came from the 1850s to the early 1920s. Many came "za chlebem" — for bread, work and a better life.
By 1900, Chicago and nearby suburbs had 23 Polish Catholic parishes, plus Polish schools and newspapers like Dziennik Chicagoski, founded in 1890.
By 1930, Polish immigrants and their children were Chicago's largest ethnic group.
The Polish Museum of America was founded in 1935 and opened to the public in 1937. Illinois made the first Monday in March Casimir Pulaski Day in 1977, first celebrated statewide in 1978.

title: The Atomic Age, 1942
hook: Under a football stadium in Chicago, the Atomic Age began quietly.
facts: On December 2, 1942, under the west stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, Enrico Fermi and his team made the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.
Their reactor, Chicago Pile-1 (CP-1), was a squash-court stack about 20 feet tall: 57 layers of graphite blocks holding uranium and uranium oxide, with cadmium rods to control it.
Step by step on December 2, the rods were pulled out. The pile went critical that afternoon at just half a watt, ran for 28 minutes, then Fermi had it shut down.
Arthur Compton reported success by phone in an improvised code: "The Italian navigator has landed in the New World." James Conant asked how the natives were. "Very friendly," Compton said.

The work proved nuclear energy could be controlled. It led toward both nuclear power and nuclear weapons. The site became a National Historic Landmark in 1965, and Henry Moore's Nuclear Energy sculpture, unveiled there in 1967, marks the spot (mentioned only — not pictured).

title: Mail Order Nation
hook: Before online shopping, a Chicago catalog let a farm family buy almost anything — even a house.
facts: In August 1872, Aaron Montgomery Ward started his Chicago mail-order business. His first catalog was a single sheet listing 163 items, with instructions for ordering by mail.

Richard W. Sears moved his mail-order watch business to Chicago in 1887 and hired watchmaker Alvah C. Roebuck. Sears, Roebuck and Co. followed in 1893, and its first large general catalog came in 1896.
Chicago was a railroad crossroads. Ward company records call the city a terminus for many railroads and ideally placed for distribution, so orders could go out by rail to customers far away.

Rural Free Delivery began as an experiment in 1896 and became permanent in 1902, bringing mail and catalogs to farm doors. Parcel Post began on January 1, 1913, so the Post Office could deliver packages too.

The big catalogs sold clothes, tools, furniture and much more. From 1908 to 1940, Sears Modern Homes even sold house kits by catalog: the first specialty house catalog appeared in 1908, and the last in 1940.

title: The First Blood Bank
hook: The words "blood bank" were born in a Chicago hospital.
facts: On March 15, 1937, Dr Bernard Fantus opened the first hospital blood bank in the United States at Cook County Hospital in Chicago, and coined the term "blood bank."
Fantus was born in Hungary in 1874 and came to the United States in 1889. He earned his medical degree in 1899 and moved to Chicago in 1902.
Before blood banks, a matching donor often had to be found and be there when a patient needed a transfusion. Stored blood meant help could be ready in advance.

Fantus built on earlier work: Oswald Robertson used stored blood at aid stations in World War I, and Fantus credited Soviet researcher Sergei Yudin in his 1937 report. Fantus reported preserving blood for 10 days.
Cook County says the blood bank cost $1,500 to open and helped with 1,354 transfusions in its first year. Storing blood for transfusion helped make modern surgery and emergency care possible.

title: Zipper, Cracker Jack & Co
hook: A zipper, a snack, a game and a gum all got their start in Chicago.
facts: On August 29, 1893, Chicago inventor Whitcomb Judson patented his "clasp locker" for shoes, and showed it at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition through the Universal Fastener Company. It was an early, often-jamming step: the smoother modern zipper came later, improved by Gideon Sundback in 1913 — not in Chicago.

In Chicago, brothers Frederick and Louis Rueckheim sold molasses-coated popcorn and peanuts. Louis found a way to keep the sweet pieces from sticking together, and in 1896 the brothers trademarked the name "Cracker Jack" and promoted it across the country.

On Thanksgiving Day, November 24, 1887, at Chicago's Farragut Boat Club, George Hancock turned a tossed boxing glove and a broom handle into "indoor baseball," with a chalked diamond and written rules. The game later became softball, and Chicago still loves its big, barehanded 16-inch version.
William Wrigley Jr. started his Chicago business in 1892, selling soap and giving chewing gum away with it. The gum won: he introduced Juicy Fruit in 1893, and Chicago became a gum and candy capital.

Palmer House tells the story this way: for the 1893 fair, Bertha Palmer asked pastry chef Joseph Sehl for a portable chocolate dessert for ladies' lunch boxes. His walnut-topped, apricot-glazed chocolate cake is still sold as the Palmer House Brownie — though it was not called a "brownie" at the time.

title: Chicago Firsts
hook: Five Chicago firsts that changed everyday life.
facts: In 1885 the Home Insurance Building rose 10 stories in Chicago. It is often called the world's first skyscraper: a tall office building held up by a fireproof metal frame, not just thick walls.
On June 6, 1892, Chicago's first "L" line opened. Small steam trains ran 3.6 miles from Congress Street to 39th Street in about 14 minutes. Much of that route is still part of the Green Line today.

On Thanksgiving Day, November 28, 1895, the Chicago Times-Herald race became the first automobile race in the United States. In snow and slush, J. Frank Duryea's motor wagon finished the roughly 54-mile Chicago–Evanston round trip at about 7 miles per hour.

On May 12, 1930, the Adler Planetarium opened to the public — the first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere. Chicago businessman Max Adler paid for the building, a Zeiss projector, and a collection of old astronomy instruments.

On April 15, 1956, Chicago station WNBQ became the first full-time color television station in the United States. All of its local live programs were broadcast in color, from studios in the Merchandise Mart.

title: The Chicago-Style Hot Dog
hook: Dragged through the garden: seven toppings, and a famous no-ketchup tradition.
facts: A Chicago-style hot dog starts simple: an all-beef frank in a steamed poppy-seed bun. Then come the "Chicago Seven": yellow mustard, neon-green relish, chopped white onion, tomato, a dill pickle spear, sport peppers, and a dash of celery salt.

The story goes back to the 1893 World's Fair. The Chicago History Museum tells how Emil Reichel and Samuel Ladany sold sausages with onions and mustard there, stayed in Chicago, and opened the store and factory that became Vienna Beef.

The full loaded style came together in hard times. During the Great Depression, vendors at Maxwell Street and other stands piled cheap vegetables onto a five-cent frank, making a small sausage feel like a full meal.
That pile of toppings earned a nickname: a hot dog "dragged through the garden." Mustard goes on first, celery salt goes on last, and every topping has its place along the bun.

And ketchup? Leaving it off is a strong Chicago tradition — many stands will not put it on a Chicago dog, and some will not serve it at all. It is a tradition, not a law: the classic recipe simply has no ketchup in it.

title: Italian Beef
hook: Thin-sliced, juicy, and dipped: a Chicago working-class sandwich.
facts: An Italian beef is slow-roasted beef, sliced very thin, piled onto a crusty Italian-style roll, and soaked with the beef's own cooking juices. Chicagoans call those juices "gravy," even though it is really a rich beef broth.

Where did it start? The story goes back to Italian immigrant weddings. Culinary historians describe "peanut weddings," where cooks slow-cooked a tough, cheap cut of beef and sliced it thin, so one roast could feed a whole hall of guests on bread.

No one inventor is proven. Al's says Al Ferreri, Frances Ferreri, and Chris Pacelli Sr. opened Al's #1 Italian Beef in Chicago in 1938 — but other families tell earlier stories, so 1938 is Al's claim, not a settled first.

Ordering has its own language. "Dipped" or "wet" means the roll itself is dipped into the hot juices. "Dry" means just a little juice. The sandwich can be soaked all the way through — many people eat it leaning over the counter.
"Hot" or "sweet"? Hot means hot giardiniera, the Chicago-style mix of pickled peppers and vegetables in oil. Sweet means roasted sweet peppers. Many regulars order both — hot and sweet together.

title: The Cubs: 108 Years
hook: They won in 1908. Then Chicago waited 108 years.
facts: The Chicago Cubs won the World Series in 1907 and again in 1908. Then the wins stopped. For more than a century, Chicago fans watched other teams lift the trophy.
The wait lasted 108 years — one of the longest title droughts in American sports — until the night of November 2, 2016, in Cleveland.
That night the Cubs beat Cleveland 8–7 in 10 innings in Game 7 of the World Series, winning the series four games to three. A 108-year wait ended in one extra-inning game.
Their home has its own long story. The ballpark on Chicago's North Side opened in 1914 as Weeghman Park. The Cubs moved in for the 1916 season, and the park took the Wrigley Field name in 1926.

In 1937 the outfield was rebuilt, and two beloved sights arrived together: a big hand-operated scoreboard, still turned by hand today, and ivy planted at the base of the outfield wall. The ivy is a mix of Boston ivy and Japanese bittersweet.

title: 1919: The Black Sox
hook: Eight players, one fixed World Series, and bans for life.
facts: In the 1919 World Series, the Chicago White Sox played the Cincinnati Reds in a best-of-nine series. Cincinnati won, five games to three, and took its first World Series title.

Soon, a darker story came out. Eight White Sox players were accused of taking money from gamblers to lose the Series on purpose: Eddie Cicotte, Joe Jackson, Chick Gandil, Swede Risberg, Buck Weaver, Happy Felsch, Lefty Williams, and Fred McMullin.
The case reached a Chicago courtroom in 1921. The players stood trial — and on August 2, 1921, a jury found them not guilty.

Baseball's answer came the very next day. Kenesaw Mountain Landis, the game's first commissioner, banned all eight players from professional baseball for life — acquittal or not, he said, players who throw games would never play again.

The bans changed baseball. Owners had hired Landis in November 1920, after the scandal broke, to restore trust in the game. The eight men never played in the major leagues again, and the 1919 team is still remembered by one name: the Black Sox.

title: Why 'The Windy City'?
hook: Wind, talk, or both? The nickname was in print long before the story most people hear.
facts: The nickname was already in print in 1876. On May 9, 1876, the Cincinnati Enquirer ran the headline "THAT WINDY CITY. Some of the Freaks of the Last Chicago Tornado" — a literal use, about real wind and a tornado in Chicago.

"Windy" also meant talkative or boastful. The Encyclopedia of Chicago notes that Chicago politicians and boosters became famous for long-winded self-promotion, so "windy" worked as a double meaning: weather, and a lot of talk.

Many early uses came from a rival city. Cincinnati and Chicago competed in the 1860s and 1870s — over meatpacking and in baseball — and "Windy City" appeared often in Cincinnati sporting news of the 1870s and 1880s as a jab at Chicago.

A popular story credits New York Sun editor Charles Dana, during the fight to host the 1893 World's Fair. But researchers have found no such Dana editorial, and the nickname was already in use in 1876 — years before that fair contest. The Dana story is not supported by the record as we have it.

And the weather? Chicago is windy, but it is not America's windiest city. In NOAA 1991–2020 climate normals, Chicago O'Hare averages about 9.7 mph — around 10 mph — while cities such as Amarillo, Texas (about 12.8 mph) average more.

title: Fort Dearborn
hook: Built in 1803, attacked in 1812, rebuilt in 1816: the fort at the river's mouth.
facts: In 1803 Captain John Whistler arrived to build a fort at the mouth of the Chicago River. It was named Fort Dearborn, for Henry Dearborn, President Jefferson’s secretary of war.
The land had come to the United States in the 1795 Treaty of Greenville. The fort stood on the south side of the river, across from DuSable’s old home on the north side.

In the War of 1812, the garrison was ordered to evacuate. On August 15, 1812, Potawatomi warriors attacked the column along the lakefront. Dozens of soldiers and civilians, and Native warriors too, were killed. The fort was burned afterward.
The army returned and rebuilt Fort Dearborn in 1816, on the same river site. Soldiers and traders came back, and settlement grew again around the fort.
Chicago still carries the fort on its flag. The star for Fort Dearborn was added on December 21, 1939 — it is the first star, nearest the pole. That is the next post’s story.

title: The Chicago Flag
hook: Two blue stripes, four red stars — and every star was added for a reason.
facts: Chicago adopted its flag on April 4, 1917. Wallace Rice, a writer and lecturer on flag design, won the city’s design competition — more than 1,000 entries were submitted.
The first flag had only two red six-pointed stars: one for the Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871, and one for the World’s Columbian Exposition of 1893.
A third star was added on October 9, 1933, for the Century of Progress exposition. A fourth was added on December 21, 1939, for Fort Dearborn — the fort in our last post.

The two blue stripes are water. The top stripe stands for Lake Michigan and the North Branch of the river; the bottom stripe, for the South Branch and the Great Canal. The white stripes stand for the North, West and South sides.
People often propose a fifth star, for floods, sports, music and more. But the official flag in Chicago’s Municipal Code still has four stars — no fifth star has been adopted.

title: Deep-Dish Pizza
hook: Born in 1943, eaten with a knife and fork: Chicago's most argued-about pizza.
facts: Chicago-style deep-dish first appeared in fall 1943, at the restaurant that became Pizzeria Uno. The Chicago History Museum dates the new style to that opening.
It is not a thicker thin pizza. Deep-dish is baked in a deep pan, with a thick crust, generous cheese and toppings, and chunky tomato sauce on top — so the cheese does not burn during the long bake.

Who invented it? No one person is proven. Ric Riccardo and Ike Sewell were behind the restaurant, and Lou Malnati worked there — later family and company stories credit different men, and historians have not settled it.
The bake is slow. The History Museum describes very hot ovens, around 600 degrees, and fifty to sixty minutes for a medium pie — one reason deep-dish is ordered ahead and eaten with a knife and fork.
Lou Malnati went his own way in time. On March 17, 1971, Lou and Jean Malnati opened the first Lou Malnati’s Pizzeria, in Lincolnwood, just outside Chicago.

title: House Music Was Born Here
hook: A Chicago club called the Warehouse gave a whole genre its name.
facts: From 1977 to 1982, a Chicago dance club called the Warehouse was the cradle of a new sound. The City of Chicago calls the building the birthplace of house music, and made it a landmark in 2023.
Frankie Knuckles, a DJ from New York, was the Warehouse’s resident DJ from 1977 to 1982. Dancers called him the Godfather of House Music.
Knuckles rebuilt songs for the dance floor: he extended and re-edited disco, R&B, soul and gospel records, and added a steady, driving beat underneath.
The name stuck to the club. Most music historians link "house" to the Warehouse — Knuckles recalled first seeing a sign, around 1980 or 1981, that said: "We play house music."
Then the sound reached vinyl. Jesse Saunders’ "On & On," recorded in 1983 and released in early 1984, is often cited as the first house record released on vinyl.

title: The Chicago Theatre
hook: Opened in 1921 as a movie palace, its C-H-I-C-A-G-O sign still lights State Street.
facts: The Chicago Theatre opened on October 26, 1921, as the Balaban and Katz Chicago Theatre. It was promoted as “The Wonder Theatre of the World,” and its first event was the silent film “The Sign on the Door,” with Norma Talmadge, a 50-piece orchestra and the Wurlitzer organ.

Architects C. W. and George L. Rapp — Rapp and Rapp — designed it in French Baroque style. The off-white glazed terra cotta front carries a miniature Arc de Triomphe above the marquee, and the lobby was modeled on the Royal Chapel at Versailles.

Its vertical sign spells C-H-I-C-A-G-O in letters about six feet tall and rises about six stories. The sign dates to 1921, but it is not untouched: early on its letters were replaced with porcelain-enamel sheet metal, and its lighting and colors changed over time.

Protection came in two steps. The theatre was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 6, 1979, and designated a Chicago Landmark on January 28, 1983. The City calls it the oldest surviving movie palace in Chicago.
After it closed in September 1985, a nine-month restoration brought it back. It reopened on September 10, 1986, with a gala performance by Frank Sinatra — and State Street had its emblem lit again.

title: Marina City
hook: Two concrete corncobs over the river — a city within a city, built to bring Chicagoans back downtown.
facts: Marina City was designed by Bertrand Goldberg Associates to draw middle-class residents back downtown. Construction officially began with a groundbreaking on November 22, 1960, on the north bank of the Chicago River.

The towers rose about one floor per day. First tenants moved into the east tower in October 1962, and both towers opened fully in early 1963 — then the tallest reinforced-concrete structures and tallest apartment buildings in the world.
The rest of the complex followed the towers. Office tenants occupied Marina City’s office building in late 1964, and the theater was finished in 1967 — the year the whole complex was completed.

Each 65-story tower stacks a 19-story parking ramp below apartments, with laundry and services between them. Semicircular balconies radiate like sunflower petals — Goldberg’s image, though Chicagoans nicknamed them corncobs. Offices, shops, a theater and a marina made it a city within a city.

Chicago protected the icon on February 10, 2016, when the City Council designated Marina City a Chicago Landmark District. More than sixty years after groundbreaking, the corncobs still anchor the riverfront.

title: The Second City
hook: Opened on December 16, 1959, a small Chicago cabaret turned improvisation into a comedy revolution.
facts: The Second City opened on December 16, 1959, at 1842 North Wells Street in Chicago. It was co-founded by Paul Sills, Howard Alk and Bernie Sahlins, who had worked in earlier Chicago companies such as the Playwrights Theatre Club and the Compass Players.

The name was a joke at Chicago’s expense. It came from A. J. Liebling’s derisive “Second City” articles about Chicago in The New Yorker in January 1952, later collected as the book Chicago: The Second City in 1952.

The method came from theater games. Paul Sills, the first director, was the son of Viola Spolin, who created the improvisational games. Sills used those games to build scenes, and Spolin later ran workshops for the Second City cast.
In 1967 the company moved to a new Chicago home at 1616 North Wells Street, in Old Town. That Wells Street home is still the Chicago home of The Second City.

The idea spread, then trained generations. A permanent Toronto base followed in 1973. Alumni lists include Tina Fey and Stephen Colbert — two names from a long line of performers who learned the craft on Second City stages.

title: Route 66 Begins in Chicago
hook: In 1926 a new national highway started in downtown Chicago and ran all the way to the Pacific.
facts: US Highway 66 was established on November 11, 1926, as part of the new numbered U.S. highway system. Signs went up along the road the following year.
It ran from Chicago to the Los Angeles area, ending near Santa Monica — about 2,400 miles through eight states: Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California.
Its original eastern end was downtown, at Jackson Boulevard and Michigan Avenue, beside the Art Institute and Grant Park.

In the late 1930s the end moved a few blocks east, to Jackson and Lake Shore Drive by Lake Michigan. After Jackson became one-way in the 1950s, westbound 66 used Adams Street — where today's "Begin Historic Route 66" sign stands. Historians note that sign marks the tradition, not the official start.

Interstates slowly replaced the old road. On June 27, 1985, US 66 was officially removed from the U.S. highway system. Today brown "Historic Route 66" signs guide travelers along surviving stretches, from Chicago across Illinois.

title: Buckingham Fountain
hook: Opened in 1927, Grant Park's great fountain was built to stand for Lake Michigan.
facts: Buckingham Fountain opened to the public on May 26, 1927, and was formally dedicated on August 26, 1927, in front of a crowd reported at about 50,000 people.
Kate Sturges Buckingham gave the fountain to Chicago in memory of her brother, Clarence Buckingham, an art collector and Art Institute trustee who died in 1913.
Architect Edward H. Bennett designed it, with French sculptor Marcel Loyau and engineer Jacques Lambert. It was inspired by the Latona Fountain at Versailles, but is about twice its size.
The fountain symbolizes Lake Michigan. Its four pairs of bronze sea horses stand for the four states that border the lake: Illinois, Wisconsin, Michigan and Indiana.
Built of pink Georgia marble, it is one of the largest fountains in the world. Its central jet can shoot water up to about 150 feet into the air.

title: Union Station
hook: Opened in 1925, Chicago's Union Station gave the railroad capital a Great Hall under a glass sky.
facts: Chicago Union Station opened for business on May 15, 1925. A formal grand opening ceremony followed on July 23, 1925.
Daniel Burnham's firm made the first design. After Burnham died in 1912, the work was finished by his successors, Graham, Anderson, Probst & White.
The Great Hall is the heart of the station. Its barrel-vaulted skylight is 219 feet long and rises about 115 feet above the floor, over columns of Roman travertine.
During World War II the skylight was blacked out for security. It was fully restored in 2018, letting natural light back into the hall.
At its peak the station handled up to 300 trains and 100,000 passengers a day. Chicago named Union Station a city landmark on May 1, 2002.

title: The Tiffany Dome
hook: Built in 1897 as Chicago's first central library, this "people's palace" hides the world's largest Tiffany glass dome.
facts: The building was completed in 1897 as Chicago's first central public library. It opened to the public in October 1897, after five years of design and construction.
The Boston firm Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge designed it, in a classical style with rare marbles, polished brass and glittering mosaics.

Its crown jewel is the Tiffany dome in Preston Bradley Hall: about 38 feet across, with some 30,000 pieces of Favrile glass, cut in the shape of fish scales. It is the largest Tiffany glass dome in the world.
The building also honored Civil War veterans: its Grand Army of the Republic rooms, completed in 1897, have a second glass dome of their own.
Chicago made the building a city landmark on November 15, 1976. It became the Chicago Cultural Center in 1991, and in 2008 the Tiffany dome was restored to let natural light shine through again.

title: Lincoln Park Zoo
hook: It began in 1868 with a gift of swans — and grew into one of America's oldest zoos, still free.
facts: Lincoln Park Zoo began in 1868, when the commissioners of New York's Central Park sent Chicago a gift: two pairs of swans.
The swans were a hit, and more animals followed. In 1874 the zoo bought its first animal — a bear cub from the Philadelphia Zoo, for $10.
In 1878 the Lincoln Park commissioners declared that the zoo must always remain free. It is still free today, one of the oldest zoos in the country.
In 1884 a bison calf was born at the zoo, reported as one of the first bison born in captivity. The Bird House opened in 1904 and is the zoo's oldest animal house still in use.
The Lion House opened in 1912. Marlin Perkins, zoo director from 1944 to 1962, brought the animals to television on the show Zoo Parade.

title: Navy Pier
hook: It opened in 1916 as Municipal Pier — a dock for ships that became Chicago's lakefront landmark.
facts: The pier opened to the public on July 15, 1916, as Municipal Pier. Architect Charles Sumner Frost designed it, based on the 1909 Plan of Chicago.
It was built for both shipping and fun: freight and passenger docks, plus halls and an auditorium. It rests on more than 20,000 wood pilings and stretches about 3,300 feet into Lake Michigan.
In 1927 Municipal Pier was renamed Navy Pier, honoring the Navy personnel who were housed there during World War I. In World War II the Navy used it again as a training center.
From 1946 to 1965 the pier was the Chicago campus of the University of Illinois. More than 100,000 students took classes there.
The headhouse and east-end auditorium became a Chicago Landmark on November 14, 1977. After a major redevelopment, Navy Pier reopened to the public in July 1995.

title: Shedd Aquarium
hook: Opened in 1930, it brought the ocean to Chicago — by train.
facts: John G. Shedd rose from the stockroom to president of Marshall Field & Company. He gave about $3 million to build an aquarium for Chicago.
Shedd died in October 1926 and saw only the architect's first drawings. Ground was broken on November 2, 1927, for a Beaux-Arts building by Graham, Anderson, Probst & White.
The aquarium officially opened on May 30, 1930. Shedd's widow, Mary R. Shedd, cut the ribbon.
It was the first inland aquarium with a permanent saltwater collection. In 1930, railroad tank cars brought about one million gallons of seawater from Key West to Chicago.
The Abbott Oceanarium opened in 1991, faced with the same white Georgia marble as the original building. The Shedd is now a National Historic Landmark.

title: Tribune Tower
hook: A 1922 contest for "the most beautiful office building in the world" gave Chicago this Gothic tower in 1925.
facts: On June 10, 1922, for its 75th anniversary, the Chicago Tribune announced an international contest for a new headquarters, with $100,000 in prize money. More than 260 entries arrived, and the winners were announced on December 3, 1922.
First prize went to New York architects John Mead Howells and Raymond Hood, for a Gothic tower.
Second prize went to Finnish architect Eliel Saarinen. His entry arrived late, but it strongly influenced skyscrapers of the later 1920s.
The tower was built from 1923 to 1925. Its crown, with flying buttresses, was modeled on the Butter Tower of Rouen Cathedral in France.
The base is studded with more than 120 stones from famous sites around the world, from the Parthenon to the Taj Mahal. Chicago named Tribune Tower a city landmark on February 1, 1989.

title: The Rookery
hook: Finished in 1888, this LaSalle Street landmark got its name from the birds that came before it.
facts: After the Great Fire of 1871, a temporary City Hall and an old water tank stood on this corner. Birds roosted there, and people called the place "the rookery" — a name that stuck to the building that replaced them. Stories about the name vary.
Burnham & Root were hired in 1885 to design a building on the site. The Rookery was completed in 1888 — eleven stories tall, one of the tallest buildings in the world at the time.
It is a transitional skyscraper: heavy load-bearing masonry walls on the outside, combined with a skeletal iron frame inside. Root's lively ornament softens the powerful exterior.
In 1905 Frank Lloyd Wright remodeled the skylit light court, covering much of the iron with gilded white marble and adding new light fixtures.
The Rookery was named a Chicago Landmark on July 5, 1972, and a National Historic Landmark on May 15, 1975. A restoration completed in 1992 brought the light court back to its 1905 look.

title: Soldier Field
hook: Opened in 1924 on the lakefront, the stadium was renamed a year later to honor America's fallen soldiers.
facts: The South Park Commission hired architects Holabird & Roche in 1919. The stadium opened on October 9, 1924, as Municipal Grant Park Stadium.
On November 11, 1925, at the urging of Chicago's Gold Star Mothers, it was renamed Soldier Field, as a memorial to U.S. soldiers who died in World War I.
In November 1926, more than 100,000 people watched Army and Navy play at Soldier Field. The game ended in a 21–21 tie.
In September 1927, about 104,000 fans saw the Jack Dempsey–Gene Tunney rematch, famous for the "long count." Tunney kept his heavyweight title.
Its double rows of Doric columns became its signature. Soldier Field was named a National Historic Landmark in 1987; the status was withdrawn in 2006 after the 2003 rebuild.

title: Garfield Park Conservatory
hook: Opened in 1908 on Chicago's West Side, it was built as "landscape art under glass."
facts: Built from 1906 and opened in 1908, it was designed by landscape architect Jens Jensen with the greenhouse firm Hitchings & Company.
It replaced three small Victorian-era greenhouses in Garfield, Douglas and Humboldt parks with one central conservatory.
Jensen shaped the front Palm House after the haystacks of the Midwestern prairie, instead of a palace or villa.
Instead of rows of potted plants, he planted directly in the ground, with lagoons, paths and layered stonework.
In the 1940s and 1950s much of it was reglazed with fiberglass; a restoration around 2000 brought back glass roofs.

title: Chicago Board of Trade Building
hook: At the end of LaSalle Street, an Art Deco tower is crowned by a faceless goddess of grain.
facts: The first Board of Trade Building on this site, designed by W. W. Boyington, opened on May 1, 1885. It was the tallest building in Chicago at the time.
Its great trading room was the heart of the grain market. By the 1920s the building had become structurally unsound, and it was demolished in 1929.
The new Art Deco building by Holabird & Root opened in 1930. Rising 44 stories, it was Chicago's tallest building on completion.
On top stands Ceres, Roman goddess of grain: a roughly 31-foot aluminum statue by John Storrs, faceless and holding wheat and corn.
It was named a Chicago Landmark on May 4, 1977, and a National Historic Landmark in 1978.

title: Riverview Park
hook: For 64 summers, an amusement park at Belmont and Western was where Chicago went to play.
facts: Riverview opened on July 2, 1904, at Belmont and Western avenues, on the grounds of a former German sharpshooters' park by the Chicago River.
It opened with just a few attractions, among them a figure-eight roller coaster and a merry-go-round.
Its most famous ride, the Bobs, opened in 1924: a wooden roller coaster with a drop of nearly 80 feet.
Riverview grew into Chicago's largest and longest-running amusement park. In October 1967 it was sold, and it never reopened.
Its 1908 carousel, built by the Philadelphia Toboggan Company, still turns at Six Flags Over Georgia and was added to the National Register in 1995.

title: Graceland Cemetery
hook: Founded in 1860, Graceland is a park-like cemetery where some of Chicago's greatest architects rest.
facts: Businessman Thomas Bryan founded Graceland in 1860 as a private, park-like cemetery just north of the city limits.
When the old City Cemetery on the lakefront was closed, many graves were moved to Graceland. That land became Lincoln Park, where the Couch Tomb still stands.
The Getty Tomb, designed by Louis Sullivan in 1890 for Carrie Eliza Getty, became a Chicago Landmark in 1971.
Lorado Taft's hooded bronze figure "Eternal Silence" (1909) marks the grave of early Chicago hotel keeper Dexter Graves.
Louis Sullivan, Daniel Burnham and Mies van der Rohe are buried here. Burnham's grave is a boulder on the small island in Lake Willowmere.

title: Glessner House
hook: Behind its fortress-like stone walls, an 1887 Prairie Avenue house hides a sunny private courtyard.
facts: Architect H. H. Richardson designed the house for farm-machinery executive John J. Glessner. It was built in 1886–1887 at Prairie Avenue and 18th Street.
Its massive, rugged stone walls were built right at the edge of the lot, unlike the other houses on Prairie Avenue at the time.
Its family rooms open onto a quiet inner courtyard, whose walls are full of doors and windows that let in light.
The Glessners filled their home with Arts and Crafts design, including William Morris wallpapers and textiles.
In 1966 preservationists bought the house for $35,000 to save it. It became a Chicago Landmark in 1970 and is now a house museum.

title: Monadnock Building
hook: Its north half, finished in 1891, is said to be the last skyscraper held up by solid brick walls.
facts: Burnham & Root designed the north half, built in 1889–1891 on Jackson Boulevard. It rises 16 stories, about 215 feet.
Its brick walls carry much of the weight and are six feet thick at the base. It is said to be the last skyscraper built with solid masonry walls.
Its brick facade has almost no ornament, which was daring for its time.
Its projecting bay windows, held up by cantilevered steel, bring extra daylight and floor space into the offices.
Holabird & Roche added a steel-frame south half in 1893. The block was planned as four buildings named for New England mountains, including Monadnock. It became a Chicago Landmark in 1973.

title: Chicago Harbor Lighthouse
hook: Since 1893, a white lighthouse has guided ships into Chicago Harbor. It is the city's last one.
facts: The lighthouse was first lit on November 9, 1893. Its conical tower is made of cast iron lined with brick.
It is the only surviving lighthouse in Chicago and one of only two left in Illinois.
It first stood at another spot on the breakwater. During the 1917 breakwater work it was moved, and its light first shone from the new site on August 1, 1918.
At the new site it gained a fog-signal building and a boathouse. Today its white tower rises between two red-roofed buildings.
The light was automated in 1979 and still marks the harbor entrance east of Navy Pier. It became a Chicago Landmark on April 9, 2003.

title: Chicago Cable Cars
hook: Long before the buses, Chicago rode to work on cars pulled by moving cables under the street.
facts: On January 28, 1882, the Chicago City Railway started cable-car service on State Street, after studying San Francisco's system.
Cable cars could not cross the river's movable bridges, so the lines used three tunnels under the Chicago River.
On the North Side, cars reached the Loop through the LaSalle Street tunnel, pulled by cable from a powerhouse built in 1887.
Chicago's lines grew to more than 80 miles, one of the largest cable systems in the world, carrying about 100,000 workers downtown a day.
Electric streetcars began replacing cable in 1892, and the last cable car ran in 1906. The LaSalle Street powerhouse became a Chicago Landmark in 2001.

title: The Iroquois Theater Fire
hook: Chicago's newest theater was sold as "absolutely fireproof." Five weeks later it became the deadliest theater fire in U.S. history.
facts: The Iroquois Theater opened on Randolph Street on November 23, 1903, and its owners advertised it as "absolutely fireproof."
On December 30, 1903, during a packed holiday matinee of Mr. Bluebeard, an arc light set a stage curtain on fire.
The asbestos fire curtain jammed, and many exits were locked, hidden behind drapes, or opened only inward.
About 602 people died, mostly women and children, the deadliest single-building fire in U.S. history.
The disaster led to laws across the country requiring public exit doors to open outward.

title: Dearborn Station
hook: Chicago's oldest surviving train station still stands at the south end of Dearborn Street, clock tower and all.
facts: Dearborn Station opened in May 1885, designed by New York architect Cyrus L. W. Eidlitz in pink granite and red brick.
At its peak it handled about 17,000 passengers a day, with the Santa Fe as its main railroad.
On December 21, 1922, a fire destroyed its steep roofs and upper floor. No one was hurt.
The Santa Fe rebuilt it with flat roofs, and trains kept running until Amtrak moved service to Union Station in 1971.
Its train shed came down in 1976, but the station became shops and offices in the 1980s and is a Chicago Landmark.

title: Essanay Studios
hook: Before Hollywood was the movie capital, Charlie Chaplin made a film on Chicago's North Side.
facts: In 1907, George K. Spoor and Gilbert M. Anderson founded a film company in Chicago and named it Essanay, for their initials, S and A.
Around 1908, Essanay moved to a new studio on Argyle Street in Uptown, where it made hundreds of films.
Anderson starred as "Broncho Billy," cinema's first cowboy hero.
Essanay signed Charlie Chaplin for $1,250 a week. He shot only one film in Chicago, His New Job (1915), with a young Gloria Swanson as an extra.
After Chaplin left and the founders fell out, Essanay collapsed in 1917. Its Argyle Street studio became a Chicago Landmark in 1996.

title: Bughouse Square
hook: For decades, anyone could climb on a box in one small Chicago park and speak to a crowd.
facts: In 1842, land developers gave the city a small plot named Washington Square. It is one of Chicago's oldest parks.
By the 1910s it had a nickname, Bughouse Square, from old slang for a mental hospital.
From the 1910s to the mid-1960s, soapbox speakers drew crowds on warm evenings. It became the nation's most famous outdoor free-speech spot.
Famous regulars included anarchist Lucy Parsons and physician Ben Reitman.
The Newberry Library, across the street, brought the soapboxes back with the Bughouse Square Debates in 1986.

title: The Masonic Temple
hook: In 1892, a 300-foot giant with steep gabled roofs rose over State Street. By 1939 it was gone.
facts: The Masonic Temple, designed by Burnham and Root, was completed in 1892 at the northeast corner of State and Randolph streets.
It stood about 302 feet tall. Sources still disagree on its stories, counting 20, 21, or 22 depending on the attic.
At the top was a glass-roofed garden and observatory where, on a clear day, visitors were said to see four states.
Shops ringed its skylit central court on the lower floors, with offices above and Masonic halls at the top.
Later called the Capitol Building, it was seen as old-fashioned and was demolished in 1939.

title: The Old Federal Building
hook: For 60 years, a domed palace in the Loop handled Chicago's mail and major federal trials.
facts: Designed by Henry Ives Cobb and completed in 1905, the Federal Building filled the block of Adams, Clark, Dearborn and Jackson, housing the federal courts and the main post office.
Shaped like a Greek cross on a high base, it was crowned by a great dome.
In 1918, in a federal courtroom in Chicago, Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis tried more than 100 leaders of the IWW labor union and sent them to prison.
On September 4, 1918, a bomb exploded at the building's Adams Street entrance, killing four people. No one was ever convicted.
The building was demolished in 1965 to make way for the Chicago Federal Center designed by Mies van der Rohe.

title: Oz Was Born in Chicago
hook: The yellow brick road started in Chicago: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz was written and published here.
facts: In 1899, Chicago writer L. Frank Baum and Chicago artist W. W. Denslow teamed up on Father Goose: His Book.
Baum, who had moved to Chicago in 1891, wrote The Wonderful Wizard of Oz in 1899 at his home on Humboldt Boulevard.
Chicago's George M. Hill Company published it in 1900 with Denslow's pictures. The first printing of 10,000 copies sold out.
In a new idea for its time, parts of the text were printed right over Denslow's drawings.
Baum turned the story into a stage musical that opened on June 16, 1902, at Chicago's Grand Opera House.

title: Provident Hospital
hook: One nursing student was turned away, so Chicago built a hospital where she could train.
facts: Around 1889, Emma Reynolds was refused by every nursing school in Chicago because she was Black. Her brother asked Dr. Daniel Hale Williams for help.
Williams and a group of Black ministers, doctors and businessmen opened Provident Hospital on May 4, 1891: 12 beds in a house at 29th and Dearborn, open to patients of all races.
In 1893, Williams operated on James Cornish, who had been stabbed near the heart, and sewed the sac around his heart. Cornish lived for more than 20 years.
In 1898, Provident moved into a new 65-bed building at 36th and Dearborn. Frederick Douglass gave to the building fund.
Provident kept training Black nurses for decades, and in 1933 it moved to a larger building on 51st Street.

title: Pinkerton Detectives
hook: A Chicago barrel maker became the detective who helped get Lincoln safely to Washington.
facts: Allan Pinkerton came from Scotland in 1842 and worked as a barrel maker (cooper) in Chicago and Dundee, Illinois.
Around 1850 he started a private detective agency in Chicago. Its motto was "We Never Sleep."
In February 1861, his agents on a railroad case found a suspected plot to kill President-elect Lincoln in Baltimore. Lincoln's route was changed so he passed through the city at night.
When the Civil War began, General George McClellan, who knew him from the Illinois Central Railroad, hired Pinkerton to run army intelligence. He signed his reports "E. J. Allen."
He returned to running his agency from Chicago, wrote popular true-crime books, and died in Chicago in 1884. He is buried at Graceland Cemetery.
